description:
I'm a solo participant interested in space, technology, electronics, and innovation. I have some experience with Arduino, ESP32, Python, OpenCV, and MediaPipe through previous projects. I'm excited to challenge myself, learn new things, and develop a creative solution for NASA Space Apps Challenge.

I'm currently participating independently and looking forward to sharing my ideas with the global community. 🚀
summary:
AstroPulse is an offline, single-file web app that helps astronauts on long-duration missions assess their own health and decide what to do when Earth cannot answer. It needs no installation or server.

A crew member records eight daily indicators: blood pressure, resting heart rate, fasting glucose, body temperature, sleep, exercise, mood and symptoms. Each reading is scored against a published reference range and compared with the astronaut's own baseline. Each field is scored as it is typed, and a blank field is never treated as healthy.

Results appear on a clickable body map whose areas are coloured by the worst reading mapped to them, each showing the NASA hazard behind it and the NASA countermeasure. Trend charts cover 7 to 30 days. The Mission Link view simulates a delayed or lost link, gives a plan for the wait, and generates a flight-surgeon report that can be queued until the link returns.

Guidance is built from NASA Human Research Program material: the five spaceflight hazards and the associated risk pages. Thresholds come from named references: NHLBI and the American Heart Association, MedlinePlus, the American Diabetes Association, the CDC and PHQ screening literature.

AstroPulse is decision support, not diagnosis. It has no sensors; the crew member enters every value.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstroPulse is a health check app for astronauts on long missions. It is one HTML file, so it runs in a browser with no internet, no installation and no server. The astronaut opens it inside the habitat and enters the day's readings: blood pressure, heart rate, fasting blood sugar, temperature, sleep, exercise minutes, a short mood screen and a list of symptoms.

Each value is scored as soon as it is typed. The app tells the astronaut what the reading means, not just whether it is good or bad. If a field is left empty it shows "not recorded" and leaves it out, because an empty box is not the same as a healthy day. If a number cannot be right, like a top blood pressure number lower than the bottom one, it asks for it again.

The body map is the main screen. It has six parts, and each part is coloured by the worst reading that belongs to it. Clicking a part shows what it does, the NASA hazard that affects it, why that measurement matters, and what NASA research lists as a countermeasure. There is a legend as well, so a grey area reads as "not measured today" instead of looking like something broke.

Two more screens. Trends shows each indicator over 7, 14 or 30 days, with the published range as one band and the astronaut's own usual range as another. Mission Link is about the delay to Earth: the link can be set to connected, delayed or lost, and the app then shows how long a reply might take, what to do while waiting, when to escalate without waiting, and a report for the flight surgeon that can be queued if the link is down.

HOW IT IS BUILT

The file has two scripts. The first is the rules engine. Every indicator has its own function that takes the reading and returns a status, a rule number and the source name. The worst status becomes the day's status, and a few combination rules turn several mild readings into one escalation. The second script is the interface.

The engine never touches the page, so I could run it on its own outside the browser. I wrote 44 test cases for the boundaries, for example 180 against 181 systolic, 125 against 126 for blood sugar, 37.3 against 37.4 for temperature, a blank field, an impossible value, and each combination rule.

Tools: HTML, CSS, plain JavaScript and SVG for the charts and the body map. No framework, no library and no build step, because anything extra would break the "open it offline" requirement. History is saved in the browser's own storage. No hardware, sensors or camera are used.

WHAT IS DIFFERENT

The one-file limit shaped the design. Because there is no internet and no install, every feature had to earn its space.

The body map is not only a traffic light. Each area carries the NASA hazard behind it, so a colour always comes with a reason.

The Mission Link screen came from the delay itself. NASA plans for up to twenty minutes one way on a Mars mission, so "contact Earth" is not always a complete answer. The screen gives the crew member something to do in that gap and produces a report the surgeon can act on later.

Every alert prints its rule number and says whether the rule comes from a published range or is the app's own safety rule. Where there is no published threshold, the app says so instead of making a number up.

WHAT WAS CONSIDERED

Safety: the app never says what condition someone has. The strongest message it gives is "outside the given range, contact the flight surgeon".

Honesty: the ranges are Earth-based because NASA publishes no public astronaut cut-off values, and the app says this on screen. Its own combination rules are labelled separately.

False alarms: a personal baseline needs three earlier readings before trends compare. Heart rate, temperature and sleep have no published emergency threshold, so they cannot turn red on their own.

Effort for the user: eight short steps, each one skippable, with the result shown as you type.

Accessibility: colour is never the only signal, the layout works on a phone, and animation switches off if the system asks for reduced motion.

Reliability: with no dependencies there is nothing to install, update or break in orbit.
dataRefs: This is the heaviest one. It gave you the countermeasures in the action plan, the symptom checklist, and almost every NASA number in the app: the 1.5 hours a day six to seven days a week, the 10–12% fitness loss, the 1–1.5% bone loss per month, the 16 sunrises, the relaxation time, the journaling.

This is the spine of the body map. Every area is labelled with one of its five hazards, and the 20-minute Mars delay that the Mission Link screen is built around comes from its Distance From Earth section.
It only supports the \"measured in spaceflight\" lines. Add it if the form wants completeness; skip it if you're keeping the list tight.
